title: Inanna and the Huluppu Tree
characters: the serpent who could not be charmed
context: One of the earliest Inanna stories, usually placed as the prologue to 'Gilgamesh, Enkidu, and the Netherworld.' Sets up Inanna as a young goddess still building her own domain and her long friendship with Gilgamesh.

beats: A single huluppu tree, uprooted by the south wind, drifts down the Euphrates.
Inanna, walking the riverbank, takes pity on the tree and plants it in her sacred garden in Uruk.
She tends it carefully for years, intending that once it is grown she will have it carved into a shining throne and a bed for herself.

But before the tree matures, it becomes infested: a serpent who cannot be charmed nests in its roots, the Anzu bird sets her young in its crown, and the dark maid Lilitu builds her house in its trunk.
Inanna weeps — she cannot bring herself to harm the tree's uninvited guests, but she cannot get her throne and bed either.
She goes to her brother Utu, the sun god, for help, but he will not act.
Inanna turns instead to Gilgamesh, the hero-king of Uruk, and tells him of her trouble.

Gilgamesh arms himself in bronze and confronts the tree: he kills the serpent, and at the sight the Anzu bird flees to the mountains with her young, and Lilitu smashes her own house and flees to the wild, uninhabited places.
Gilgamesh's men fell the huluppu tree and strip its trunk.
From the wood, Gilgamesh has a throne and a bed made for Inanna, exactly as she wished.
In gratitude, Inanna gives Gilgamesh two gifts made from the tree's roots and crown: the pukku (a drum) and the mikku (its drumsticks) — objects that will matter again later in his story.
The tale closes with Inanna's garden restored to order, and a bond of favor established between the goddess and the king of Uruk.

title: Inanna and Enki: The Theft of the Mes
context: Enki, god of wisdom and the fresh waters of the Abzu, holds the mes — the hundred-plus divine decrees underlying civilization, kingship, and the arts. Inanna wants them for her city, Uruk.

beats: Inanna decides Uruk deserves the mes and travels to Enki's city, Eridu, and his house in the Abzu.
Enki, delighted by his daughter-like guest, orders his minister Isimud to welcome her with a great feast, and calls for beer — cup after cup, toasted between the two of them.

As Enki grows pleasantly, grandly drunk, he begins — as a boastful host — to bestow the mes on Inanna one by one: the arts of priesthood and kingship, truth, descent and ascent from the underworld, the crafts, music, the art of writing, and dozens more.
Inanna accepts each one and has them loaded onto her Boat of Heaven, docked outside.
Once the boat is fully laden, she says her farewells and sets off upriver toward Uruk while Enki is still deep in his cups.
Enki sobers up and asks Isimud where the mes have gone; Isimud tells him he gave them all to Inanna, and that she has already sailed for Uruk.
Horrified, Enki sends Isimud and a series of sea monsters to chase down the Boat of Heaven and seize it at each stopping point along the way.
At every quay, the monsters try to take the boat; each time, Inanna's minister and steadfast helper Ninshubur beats them back and the boat sails on.
The boat and its cargo of mes reach Uruk safely, and Inanna unloads them at the White Quay in full view of her people, making the gift irreversible and public.
Enki, defeated, reconciles himself to what has happened and even sends further blessings after her — acknowledging that the mes now belong to Uruk.

title: Inanna Takes Command of Heaven
context: A shorter, more fragmentary hymn-narrative about Inanna asserting her claim to the Eanna temple precinct in Uruk — literally 'House of Heaven.'

beats: Inanna sets her heart on ruling over the Eanna, the great temple precinct that is heaven's house on earth, and on being recognized among the Anuna gods as their equal.
She crosses the marshes and waterways toward the temple, undeterred by the difficulty of the crossing.
The surviving text is fragmentary, but it moves toward Inanna successfully claiming her place: the Eanna becomes hers, and her authority over it is acknowledged by the other gods.
The hymn functions as a founding claim: it explains, mythically, why the Eanna in Uruk belongs to Inanna and why her cult there is legitimate and ancient.

title: The Courtship of Inanna and Dumuzi
context: Often called 'Inanna Prefers the Farmer' — a marriage-debate poem that ends in Inanna's wedding to Dumuzi, a story full of pastoral courtship imagery later associated with the sacred marriage rite (hieros gamos).

beats: Utu tells his sister Inanna it is time she married, and proposes Dumuzi the shepherd as a husband.
Inanna resists, declaring she prefers the farmer Enkimdu — who can offer her flax for linen, grain, beans, and a house full of produce.
Dumuzi, offended, argues his own case directly to Inanna: he claims the shepherd has everything the farmer has, and more besides — milk, cream, cheese, wool, and the richness of the herds.

Enkimdu, rather than fighting Dumuzi for Inanna's hand, graciously steps back, offering Dumuzi his friendship and even inviting him to his wedding feast, and promising the farmer's goods to Dumuzi's flocks freely.
Inanna, won over by Dumuzi's case and his devotion, agrees to be his bride.
Dumuzi comes to Inanna's house/gate with gifts and is welcomed in by Inanna's mother, Ningal.
Inanna bathes and adorns herself for her beloved, and the two exchange tender, sensuous love-songs celebrating each other's bodies, the bed strewn with sweet herbs, and the joy of the marriage bed.
Their union is treated as more than personal: it is tied to the fertility of the land itself — Dumuzi's kingship and the abundance of Sumer's fields and flocks are secured by this marriage.
The wedding is celebrated with feasting, and Inanna is enthroned beside Dumuzi as his queen.
The poem closes on the couple's joy — a joy the later myths (Inanna's Descent, Dumuzi's Dream) will complicate.

title: The Descent of Inanna to the Underworld
characters: Ereshkigal (her older sister, Queen of the Underworld)
context: The single most important and best-known Inanna myth: her journey to her sister's realm, her death, and her return at a terrible price. Usually the emotional centerpiece of any Inanna cycle.

beats: Inanna decides to descend to the Great Below, the realm ruled by her older sister Ereshkigal — the myth gives little reason beyond her own will to go.

Before leaving, she instructs her faithful minister Ninshubur: if Inanna does not return in three days, Ninshubur must go to the gods — Enlil, then Nanna, then finally Enki — and beg them to rescue her.
Inanna dresses in her full divine regalia: the crown, lapis beads, a breastplate, a golden ring, a lapis measuring rod, and the royal robe — the me of her power worn as ornament.

At the outer gate of the underworld, the gatekeeper Neti challenges her; Ereshkigal, hearing of her sister's approach, is furious and orders that Inanna be let in — but only through the seven gates, one at a time.

At each of the seven gates, Inanna is made to remove one piece of her regalia — the crown, the beads, the breastplate, the ring, the rod, the robe — until at the seventh gate she stands before her sister naked and bowed low, stripped of all her power.
The seven judges of the underworld, the Anuna, fix their eyes of death on Inanna and pronounce judgment against her; Ereshkigal turns her own eye of death on her sister.
Inanna is struck dead and her corpse is hung on a hook on the wall, like a piece of meat.

Three days and three nights pass; when Inanna does not return, Ninshubur does exactly as instructed — she mourns and then goes to Enlil and Nanna, both of whom refuse to interfere in the underworld's affairs.
Finally Ninshubur goes to Enki, who is genuinely grieved and resourceful: he scrapes dirt from under his fingernails and fashions two small sexless creatures, the kurgarra and the galatur.

He gives them the food and water of life and sends them into the underworld, instructing them to slip in unseen and to sympathize with Ereshkigal, who they will find in the pain of mourning her own losses — echoing her every groan.
Moved that someone finally shares her grief, Ereshkigal offers them a gift; they ask only for the rotting corpse on the hook, sprinkle it with the food and water of life, and Inanna revives.

The law of the underworld will not simply let Inanna leave: no one may ascend from the Great Below without leaving someone behind in their place. Demons, the galla, are sent up with her to find her replacement.
Inanna, escorted by the galla, first finds Ninshubur mourning for her in sackcloth at the city gate; she refuses to give the demons her loyal minister.
She passes through several other cities and finds her sons/attendants also in mourning; she spares each of them in turn.
Finally she comes to Uruk and finds Dumuzi — her husband — not mourning at all, but dressed in splendid robes, seated on her own throne as if nothing has happened.

Enraged, Inanna fixes the eye of death on Dumuzi herself and hands him over to the galla as her replacement; he pleads for his life and tries to escape, transformed by Utu into a snake, but is ultimately caught.
The myth ends on this harsh judgment, setting up the grief and bargaining that follows in Dumuzi's Dream.

title: Dumuzi's Dream
context: The direct sequel to the Descent: Dumuzi's flight from the demons, and the bargain that finally softens Inanna's sentence into the changing of the seasons.

beats: Before the demons ever reach him, Dumuzi has an ominous dream: reeds rising and crying out against him, his churn overturned, his cup fallen, his shepherd's crook consumed, a falcon seizing a lamb from the fold.
Shaken, he asks his sister Geshtinanna to interpret it; she tells him plainly that the dream means galla demons are coming to drag him to the underworld in place of Inanna.
Sure enough, the galla arrive, relentless and without pity, hunting Dumuzi across the countryside.
Dumuzi begs Utu, the sun god (brother-in-law to them both, married to Inanna's circle), for help; Utu changes his hands and feet, letting him escape like a snake through several hiding places.
Geshtinanna hides her brother and, when the galla seize and torture her for his location, refuses again and again to betray him.
In the end it is not Geshtinanna but a false friend who gives up his hiding place, and the demons finally corner and seize Dumuzi.
Geshtinanna, grieving, searches everywhere for her brother's body and eventually comes before Inanna herself to plead on his behalf.

Moved by Geshtinanna's devotion and her own grief at what her judgment has cost, Inanna decrees a compromise: Dumuzi will spend half the year in the underworld, and Geshtinanna will voluntarily take his place for the other half, so neither is bound there forever.
This yearly exchange becomes the mythic explanation for the seasons — the dying and returning of vegetation and flocks tied to Dumuzi's absence and return.

title: Inanna and Shukaletuda
context: A darker myth dealing with violation and retribution, and — read astronomically — with the motions of the planet Venus across the sky.

beats: Shukaletuda is a gardener who tends his plot poorly; his one success is a single unusual poplar tree with especially wide-spreading branches that he keeps watered and shaded.
Exhausted, Inanna lies down to rest in his garden, beneath that same tree, after a long journey across heaven and earth.
While she sleeps, Shukaletuda comes upon her and rapes her, then flees back into the city crowds to hide among ordinary people.

Inanna wakes and realizes what has been done to her; enraged and grieving, she sets out to find her attacker and unleashes plagues and disasters on the land — blood in the wells, storms, and other calamities — trying to flush him out.
Shukaletuda, terrified, goes to his father for advice and hides among his brothers in the city, then in the mountains, always staying one step ahead of Inanna's search.

The text describes Inanna's hunt in language that mirrors Venus's actual movements through the sky — rising, setting, and sweeping across the heavens in search of her attacker, an early astronomical myth encoded in narrative.
Shukaletuda pleads that killing him will not undo what was done and that he already regrets it, but Inanna is unmoved in her pursuit of justice.
Eventually she finds him and passes final judgment, ending his life for the crime.

The myth closes with Inanna's authority over sexual violation and personal violation established firmly: she is not only a goddess of love, but one who avenges harm done to her, even at great cost to the land in the meantime.

title: Inanna and Mount Ebih
context: A hymn of conquest: Inanna asserts her supremacy over a mountain range that refuses to bow to her or to any god.

beats: Mount Ebih stands proud and unbowed, refusing the authority of any god, its slopes lush and untouched, considering itself beyond judgment.
Inanna, offended by this open defiance, demands that An, king of the gods, let her destroy the mountain to prove her power; An warns her that Ebih is dangerous and advises against it.
Undeterred, Inanna arms herself and attacks Ebih directly — hurling fire, poison, and storm against its slopes.
She tears down its forests, dries up its rivers, and breaks its peaks, humbling the mountain completely.

Ebih, defeated, submits to her; Inanna declares that no place, however proud or remote, stands outside her authority, and the hymn ends celebrating her as a warrior equal to any god in the pantheon, not merely a goddess of love and fertility.

title: Inanna and Bilulu
context: A lesser-known lament-and-revenge story tying together Inanna's grief over Dumuzi with an act of justice against those who harmed him.

beats: Dumuzi, tending his flocks in open country far from the safety of the city, is killed — in this telling, at the hands of the old woman Bilulu and, in some versions, her son Girgire, bandits of the wild steppe.
Inanna, learning of her husband's death, is consumed by grief and mourns him bitterly, wandering the countryside where he died.
Her grief turns to a demand for justice: she tracks down those responsible for his death.

Inanna transforms Bilulu (and, in some versions, her household) into spirits of the wasteland — figures associated with drink-offerings and the wilderness left behind by his loss — a punishment that is also a kind of eternal memorial to what was taken from her.
The story reinforces Inanna's role as a griever who does not let violence against those she loves go unanswered, echoing the same fierce justice she shows in Inanna and Shukaletuda.

title: Ishtar and Gilgamesh: The Bull of Heaven
context: From Tablet VI of the later Akkadian Epic of Gilgamesh — by this point Inanna is known by her Akkadian name Ishtar. A dramatic turn from the old friendship shown in the Huluppu Tree story.

beats: Fresh from his victory over the monster Humbaba, Gilgamesh washes and dresses himself in splendor; seeing him, Ishtar is overcome with desire and proposes marriage, promising him a golden chariot, cedar palaces, and the homage of kings and nations.
Gilgamesh refuses her bluntly and cruelly, listing off her previous lovers — Dumuzi and others — and the ruin that befell each of them, essentially accusing her of destroying everyone she has loved.

Humiliated and enraged before the other gods, Ishtar goes to her father An and demands he give her the Bull of Heaven to punish Gilgamesh, threatening to break open the gates of the underworld and let the dead overrun the living if he refuses.
An warns her that the Bull of Heaven's release will bring seven years of famine, but relents and gives her the reins.
Ishtar leads the Bull of Heaven down into Uruk, where its snorting alone opens great pits in the earth that swallow hundreds of the city's men.
Gilgamesh and his companion Enkidu fight the bull together; Enkidu seizes it by the horns and tail while Gilgamesh drives his sword between its neck and shoulder, killing it.
Ishtar, watching from the city walls, curses Gilgamesh for the bull's death; Enkidu, in fury, tears a haunch from the bull's carcass and hurls it at her, adding further insult.

The people of Uruk celebrate the heroes' victory, but this triumph carries a price: the gods decree that one of the two men must die for the killing of the bull and the earlier death of Humbaba — and the sentence falls on Enkidu, setting in motion the grief that drives the rest of the Gilgamesh epic.
The episode marks Inanna/Ishtar at her most dangerous and wounded-pride-driven, a sharp contrast to the goddess who once rewarded this same city's king with a throne and bed.

title: The Exaltation of Inanna (Nin-me-sara)
context: Not a myth in the narrative sense but the oldest surviving work by a named author in world literature — a personal hymn of appeal, composed by the Akkadian princess-priestess Enheduanna, daughter of Sargon of Akkad.

beats: Enheduanna, high priestess of the moon god Nanna at Ur and daughter of Sargon of Akkad, is driven from her temple and city when the rebel Lugal-Ane seizes power and she refuses to legitimize him.
Exiled and in danger, she composes this hymn not as detached mythology but as a desperate, personal appeal — addressing Inanna directly, in her own voice, as 'I, Enheduanna.'

The hymn opens by praising Inanna in overwhelming terms: as the one who received her powers directly from An, king of the gods, and who now holds authority over heaven, earth, and the assembly of the gods themselves — more supreme, in this telling, than any other deity.

Enheduanna describes Inanna's fury as a storm that flattens mountains, floods cities, and terrifies even the other gods, establishing beyond question that this is a goddess capable of righting the wrong done to her priestess.
She lays out her own suffering plainly: stripped of her office, exiled from the temple she served, treated as an enemy in the very city she once served faithfully.

The hymn closes with Inanna's power restored and celebrated, and — per the historical/legendary tradition around this composition — Enheduanna's own position eventually vindicated, her exile ended by the goddess she praised.
As the first authored text in human history with a named writer, this hymn is also the moment Inanna's cult and Enheduanna's own voice become permanently fused in the historical record.
